clue.text: Poet's occasional work about University church

indicators.note: Wrapping one thing about another puts it round the outside, so the short pieces land in the middle of the longer one.

parts.note: a char is an odd job done now and then, the charwoman's word for casual domestic work
U is the standard short form for university
CE, the Church of England, is the crossword's church

explanation.surface: A poet picking up casual work for a university chapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasional work' looks like a dig at how little a poet writes, and it is really the charwoman's noun: a stint of odd jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales in verse and is the poet English literature starts with, so 'Poet' names him by his trade.

clue.text: Stop copper taking on aggressive salesman

indicators.note: To take something on is to take it aboard, so what follows is added onto the letters already there.

parts.note: CU is the chemical symbol for copper
a tout is the one who pushes tickets at you outside the ground

explanation.surface: A policeman signing up a pushy salesman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is the metal here, not the policeman the salesman in the surface is asking you to picture.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut out is what an engine does when it stops dead, so 'Stop' is the intransitive verb — quit, pack in — rather than an order.

clue.text: Information spiking a US lawyer's expected work

indicators.note: To spike a thing is to drive a point straight through it, so these letters end up pushed into the middle of the words beside them.

parts.note: the clue's own indefinite article, taken across as a letter
DA is the District Attorney, the prosecutor in an American court
gen is British slang for the information you need — 'give me the gen' — out of forces use

explanation.surface: A leak of information landing on an American prosecutor's list of jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spiking' reads as a newsdesk word — a story spiked is a story killed — and the instruction it carries is impaling one word on another.
explanation.definitionFit: Agenda is Latin for 'things to be done', so it names the work a meeting is expected to get through, item by item.

clue.text: Add something to study, with a lot of attempts to suppress objection

parts.note: to con a text is to study it closely, an old sense crosswords keep alive

indicators.note: To suppress something is to hold it down out of sight, and out of sight here means inside the letters that close over it.

parts.note: attempts are tries, and a lot of that word is all of it bar the final letter
the word an objection begins with: 'but…'

explanation.surface: Someone told to add to their research while an objection is shouted down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' is a verb, not a room, and the objection is clued by the one word everybody raises an objection with.
explanation.definitionFit: To contribute is to add something to a common pot — money, an idea, a chapter — so the definition is the plain action the verb names.

clue.text: Take another exam? Refuse, dismissing an opening from school

indicators.note: To dismiss someone is to send them away, so the letter named next leaves the word altogether.

parts.note: to resist an order is to refuse it, and this is the word before anything is taken out

indicators.note: An opening is where a thing starts, so this asks for the letter its word opens with.

parts.note: school opens with S, and that is the letter dismissed

explanation.surface: A candidate refuses, and a place at the school is taken off the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' is the verb stressed on its second syllable, not the rubbish a school might have cleared, and 'an opening' is one letter rather than a vacancy.
explanation.definitionFit: A resit is the paper you take again after failing it, and the question mark admits the definition is a description rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Minion whips another minion endlessly

parts.note: the cat-o'-nine-tails was the navy's flogging whip, so whips are cats
a pawn is the lowest piece on the board and the errand-runner of the metaphor, and its end is dropped

explanation.surface: One underling flogging another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minion' is used twice on purpose, once as definition and once as the chess pawn, and the answer comes from the fable of the monkey using the cat's paw to rake chestnuts out of the fire.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat's-paw is someone used as a tool by another, which is a minion in the exact sense of a dupe sent to do the dirty work.

clue.text: Islands' postal service getting a source of protection

parts.note: islands strung out in a line are called a chain, as the Hawaiian ones are
the mail is what the postal service carries, and in Britain what it is called

explanation.surface: An island post office throwing in something that keeps you safe.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words that read as one idea — the islands' mail — turn out to be separate pieces, and the second is the armourer's spelling, from the French maille, a ring of mesh.
explanation.definitionFit: Chain mail is the linked metal mesh a soldier wore into battle, so the definition is protection in the literal, wearable sense.

clue.text: What actor seeks has turned up — something on the stage?

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned up means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards

parts.note: an actor goes after a part, a role in a play

explanation.surface: An actor auditioning finally lands the role he was after, then appears on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has turned up' looks like the actor arriving, but it reverses PART. The definition is a trapdoor in a stage floor, through which performers can appear or vanish.
explanation.definitionFit: A trap is a hinged opening set into a theatre's floor, used for sudden entrances and exits.

clue.text: Indicates remaining bits under computer socket

indicators.note: This entry runs down the page, so the piece said to be under the other is written below it, second.

parts.note: a port is the socket you plug a cable into on the side of a machine
the bits left over at the finish are the ends, as in odds and ends

explanation.surface: Spare scraps of hardware sitting beneath a computer's socket.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay are computing words on the surface, and the definition is the one thing here with nothing to do with machines: an omen.
explanation.definitionFit: To portend is to be a sign of what is coming, which is what 'indicates' means when a thing rather than a person does it.

clue.text: No great confusion, we hear, when most are at work

indicators.note: What follows is reported by ear, so it is the noise of the words that counts and not their spelling.

parts.note: something no great shakes is weak, and that noise is written down this other way
the confusion you are left in is a daze, and said aloud it is spelt like this

explanation.surface: No great muddle, apparently, on the days when most people are working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No great' has to be heard as a single adjective before the sound-alike will work, which is why neither half looks anything like the word it came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Weekdays are Monday to Friday, so the definition names them by the one thing nearly everybody does on them.

clue.text: Male accessory — popular marketing move

parts.note: the strip of silk knotted at a man's collar
what is popular this season is in — the crossword's usual two letters for fashionable

explanation.surface: Something a man wears with a shirt, and a bright idea for shifting more of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash does all the hiding: it reads as a pause between two thoughts and is really the join between two pieces of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie-in is the mug or the toy sold on the back of a film, so 'marketing move' is the trade's own description of it.

clue.text: Rakes active around a block turned over in prehistoric site

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit around the next piece
being active means busy and moving about, so the letters of rakes are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so the word for block is read backwards

parts.note: to bar is to block

explanation.surface: Someone vigorously raking the ground turns up a stone block at an ancient dig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'active' rearranges RAKES into SKRAE; 'turned over' makes BAR into RAB, so A plus RAB gives ARAB, and 'around' puts SKRAE around it. Skara Brae is a Neolithic village in Orkney, off northern Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Skara Brae is a Stone Age settlement of stone houses, preserved in sand on the Orkney mainland.

clue.text: Get where sports ground security might not find you?

parts.note: the place a sweep of the ground would miss is beneath something, and beneath is this word
'where' asks for a place at a sports ground, and the banked seating along one side is the stand

explanation.surface: A tip on where to hide from the stewards at a football ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get' is the definition and the only part of the clue not about football; everything after it is one picture, a hiding place a steward would walk straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: To understand something is to get it, in the everyday 'I get it' sense of a penny dropping rather than of obtaining anything.

clue.text: Stop, exhausted, toppling over, nothing less

indicators.note: less means minus, so the letter that stands for nothing is taken away
something toppling over ends up the other way round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: done in the sense of worn out, as in 'I'm done'
O, the round figure zero, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: An exhausted person, about to collapse, is told to stop before they fall over with nothing left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'toppling over' reverses DONE into ENOD, and 'less' removes the O (nothing) from it.
explanation.definitionFit: To end something is to bring it to a stop, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Pretty US lawyer, busy imprisoning Republican

indicators.note: To imprison someone is to shut them inside walls, so the letter named is locked in between the pieces either side.

parts.note: an American attorney is shortened to att, as on a law firm's letterhead
somebody busy is active, out doing things
R is the letter printed beside an American politician's name when they sit on that side

explanation.surface: A hard-working American lawyer with a Republican locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty' stands exactly where an adjective describing the lawyer would stand, which is what makes it so easy to read as part of the picture instead of as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Attractive means good-looking, and 'Pretty' is the everyday word for it — the adjective, not 'pretty' meaning fairly.

clue.text: Leads by running around region unthinkingly?

indicators.note: the rearranged letters wrap around the region
running loose means out of order, so the letters of the two words are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange
a tract is a region or stretch of land

explanation.surface: A race leader wins by a margin while running around a district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running' rearranges LEADS BY into ABSEDLY, and 'around' puts that around TRACT. The question mark flags that absent-mindedness is only one way of acting without thought.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting abstractedly means with one's mind elsewhere, preoccupied and not paying attention, hence without thinking.

clue.text: Those people seen around shady area where New York drunks gather

indicators.note: To be seen around a place is to be all over it, so this word goes right round the one beside it.

parts.note: those people over there are they, and the word splits to let something in
a bower is the leafy shelter in a garden, shady in the literal sense

explanation.surface: Locals loitering round a disreputable patch of the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shady' is the trap: it wants to mean disreputable, to match the drunks, and it means full of leaves — a bower is a garden arbour.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bowery is the Manhattan street that became America's byword for flophouses and skid row, so the definition names it by its old reputation.

clue.text: Flush sewage after Australian takes over leadership

indicators.note: Taking over the leadership is stepping into the top job, so this letter replaces the one standing at the front.

parts.note: effluent is the waste liquid a treatment works discharges, the technical word for sewage
A is the short form for Australian, and it is the letter moving in

explanation.surface: Sewage flushed away once an Australian has taken charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flush' is the definition and it means rolling in money, not the lavatory flush that the sewage beside it is pushing you towards.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody flush is well supplied with cash for the moment, which is what affluent means: wealthy, in funds.

clue.text: Medic to leave, upset, with woozy head? It's the port

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor, a medic

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to go is to leave

indicators.note: feeling woozy is feeling dizzy and muddled, so the letters of head are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A doctor feeling unsteady and dizzy wants to go home, perhaps after too much port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses GO into OG and 'woozy' rearranges HEAD into HEDA. The port is not the drink but Drogheda, a harbour town on Ireland's east coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Drogheda is a seaport town on the River Boyne estuary in County Louth, Ireland.

clue.text: Naval leader: source for support for idle tars, possibly

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters may be arranged some other way
the source of a word is where it begins, so its first letter is taken

parts.note: its first letter is S
taken as written, as letters to rearrange
taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An admiral provides the backing for lazy sailors, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'source for' takes S from support; add FOR IDLE TARS and 'possibly' rearranges the lot. The First Sea Lord is the professional head of Britain's Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: The First Sea Lord is the senior serving officer who commands the Royal Navy, its top admiral.

clue.text: Delicate sex? Mostly safe to accept that

indicators.note: To accept something is to take it in, and 'that' points back at the two letters just named, so they go inside.

parts.note: a peter is a safe in old criminal slang — cracking one is blowing a peter — and most of it stops short of the last letter
IT is sex appeal, from the 1920s It girl

explanation.surface: The delicate sex, and whether it is still safe to accept the description.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's question mark half-apologises for 'the delicate sex', and the safe is the burglar's kind rather than the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Petite describes a woman as small and finely built, which is 'delicate' in the sense of slight rather than fragile.

clue.text: Immature supporter interrupting international

definitions.note: 'Immature' is an adjective where the answer is usually a noun; the setter is allowed it because the noun works attributively too — an infant industry is an immature one.

indicators.note: To interrupt is to cut in part-way through, so this piece breaks into the middle of the word beside it.

parts.note: INT is the standard short form for international, as on a fixture list
a supporter at a match is a fan

explanation.surface: A very young fan barging into an international fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' in a crossword is usually a bra or a pillar, and here it is the ordinary one: the fan standing in the crowd that 'international' has already put you in.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant is at the earliest stage of growing, so 'immature' names the state exactly: not yet grown rather than childish in behaviour.

clue.text: Taking considerable time, missing new record

indicators.note: missing means without, so the letter for new is dropped

parts.note: something long takes a lot of time

explanation.surface: A slow process that takes ages still fails to set a new record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing' takes the N (new) out of LONG. 'record' looks like a world record, but here it is a written record, such as a ship's log.
explanation.definitionFit: A log is a written record of events, such as a ship's daily journal of its voyage.

clue.text: Very good noodle soup, wholesome, suitable for a poet

parts.note: so tired, so good: 'so' is the everyday intensifier standing in for very
pho is the Vietnamese beef-and-noodle soup, eaten there for breakfast
clean living is wholesome living, and a clean joke is a wholesome one

explanation.surface: A verdict on a bowl of noodle soup: very good, healthy, the sort of thing a poet would order.
explanation.walkthrough: Sophocles is the Athenian tragedian of Oedipus and Antigone, and the adjective made out of his name is what the definition is reaching for.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophoclean means in the manner of Sophocles, so the definition points not at poetry in general but at the adjective one poet's name gives.

clue.text: River goes under trendy home of theologian

indicators.note: This entry runs down the page, so what goes under the other piece is written below it, second.

parts.note: what is trendy is hip, a word that has meant fashionable since the jazz age
the Po is the long river of northern Italy, a crossword regular

explanation.surface: A river running beneath a fashionable theologian's house.
explanation.walkthrough: Augustine took his name from the North African city he was bishop of, so 'home' here is a town rather than a house.
explanation.definitionFit: Hippo was the Roman city in North Africa where Augustine was bishop, so the definition names a town by its most famous resident.

clue.text: Dislike son abandoning expedition

indicators.note: abandoning means leaving behind, so the letter for son is dropped from the word

parts.note: expedition in its old sense of promptness or speed, which is haste
S is the abbreviation for son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A father resents his son for deserting the family on a trip abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoning' takes S (son) out of HASTE. 'expedition' suggests a journey, but here it means speed, as in 'with all expedition'.
explanation.definitionFit: To hate something is to feel intense dislike for it, so the two verbs are near synonyms.

clue.text: Caught one to create mascara?

indicators.note: To catch what somebody said is to hear it, so the word beside this is taken by ear and written down as it sounds.

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I, and said aloud that letter is spelt this way
to make something up is to invent or create it

explanation.surface: Somebody caught in the act of inventing a mascara.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' is the hearing kind, as in 'I didn't catch that', so the Roman numeral is what you say out loud and the question mark admits mascara is only one sort of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Mascara is one product in the eye make-up family, so the definition works by example — hence the question mark — rather than as a synonym.

clue.text: Bass in zone 2 recalled area of party island?

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters are read backwards
the bass letter goes inside the next pieces

parts.note: II is 2 in Roman numerals
B is the abbreviation for bass, as in a choir's SATB

explanation.surface: Sound system in a club, zone two, gets recalled from a rave area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts B inside Z plus II to give ZIBI; 'recalled' reverses it to IBIZ, then A follows. Ibiza is a Spanish Balearic island famed for clubbing.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibiza, in the Balearics, is famous for its nightclubs and all-night dance parties, so is a party island.

clue.text: Getting on in attempt to produce something of Shakespeare?

indicators.note: 'in' is doing literal work: the letters before it go bodily inside the word that follows.

parts.note: an attempt is a try, and the word opens up to take something inside
someone getting on in years has aged

explanation.surface: An ageing actor having a go at staging some Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting on' is about years, not about progress or about getting along with people, and the question mark is there because the answer is a whole class of the plays rather than one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's plays divide into comedies, histories and tragedies, so the definition names one of those categories by example.

clue.text: Finished end of route at gorge

parts.note: when a match is finished it is over

indicators.note: The end of a word is its last letter, and that single letter is all this takes.

parts.note: the last letter of route
the clue's own preposition, lifted out letter for letter

explanation.surface: Reaching the far end of the road at a ravine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gorge' is a verb here, and the surface spends its whole length making it a landscape feature at the end of a walk.
explanation.definitionFit: To gorge is to stuff yourself well past the point of sense, which is what overeating is; the ravine is the surface's other noun.
